trans-unit.source: <g id="_0">FINIS.</g>
<g id="_0">Executive Director's Notes:</g>
<g id="_0">So. . .with this caveat. . .we have NOT changed the canon errors, here is the Project Gutenberg Etext of Shakespeare's The first Part of Henry the Sixt.</g>
<g id="_0"> Snug.

Haue you the Lions part written? pray you if<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
be, giue it me, for I am slow of studie<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Quin.

You may doe it extemporie, for it is nothing<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
but roaring<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Bot.
Let mee play the Lyon too, I will roare that I will doe any mans heart good to heare me.
I will roare, that I will make the Duke say, Let him roare againe, let him roare againe</g>
<g id="_0"> Quin.
If you should do it too terribly, you would fright the Dutchesse and the Ladies, that they would shrike, and that were enough to hang us all</g>
<g id="_0"> All.
That would hang vs euery mothers sonne</g>
<g id="_0"> Bottome.

I graunt you friends, if that you should fright the Ladies out of their Wittes, they would haue no more discretion but to hang vs: but I will aggrauate my voyce so, that I will roare you as gently as any sucking Doue; I will roare and 'twere any Nightingale</g>
<g id="_0"> Quin.
You can play no part but Piramus, for Piramus is a sweet-fac'd man, a proper man as one shall see in a summers day; a most louely Gentleman-like man, therfore you must needs play Piramus</g>
<g id="_0"> Bot.
Well, I will vndertake it.

What beard were I<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
best to play it in?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Quin.
Why, what you will<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Bot.
I will discharge it, in either your straw-colour beard, your orange tawnie beard, your purple in graine beard, or your French-crowne colour'd beard, your perfect yellow</g>
<g id="_0"> Quin.
Some of your French Crownes haue no haire at all, and then you will play bare-fac'd.

But masters here are your parts, and I am to intreat you, request you, and desire you, to con them by too morrow night: and meet me in the palace wood, a mile without the Towne, by Moone-light, there we will rehearse: for if we meete in the Citie, we shalbe dog'd with company, and our deuises knowne.
In the meane time, I wil draw a bil of properties, such as our play wants.
I pray you faile me not</g>

<g id="_0">Michael S. Hart<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Project Gutenberg<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Executive Director<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Bottom.
We will meete, and there we may rehearse more obscenely and couragiously.
Take paines, be perfect, adieu</g>
<g id="_0"> Quin.
At the Dukes oake we meete</g>
<g id="_0"> Bot.
Enough, hold or cut bow-strings.</g>
<g id="_0">Exeunt.</g>
<g id="_0">Actus Secundus.</g>
<g id="_0">Enter a Fairie at one dore, and Robin goodfellow at another.</g>
<g id="_0"> Rob.
How now spirit, whether wander you?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Fai.

Ouer hil, ouer dale, through bush, through briar,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Ouer parke, ouer pale, through flood, through fire,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
I do wander euerie where, swifter then y Moons sphere;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
And I serue the Fairy Queene, to dew her orbs vpon the green.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>

The Cowslips tall, her pensioners bee,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
In their gold coats, spots you see,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Those be Rubies, Fairie fauors,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
In those freckles, liue their sauors,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
I must go seeke some dew drops heere,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
And hang a pearle in euery cowslips eare.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>

Farewell thou Lob of spirits, Ile be gon,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
Our Queene and all her Elues come heere anon<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Rob.

The King doth keepe his Reuels here to night,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Take heed the Queene come not within his sight,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
For Oberon is passing fell and wrath,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
Because that she, as her attendant, hath<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
A louely boy stolne from an Indian King,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
She neuer had so sweet a changeling,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
And iealous Oberon would haue the childe<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Knight of his traine, to trace the Forrests wilde.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>

But she (perforce) with-holds the loued boy,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
Crownes him with flowers, and makes him all her ioy.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>

And now they neuer meete in groue, or greene,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>
By fountaine cleere, or spangled star-light sheene,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
But they do square, that all their Elues for feare<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/>
Creepe into Acorne cups and hide them there<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_14"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Fai.

Either I mistake your shape and making quite,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Or else you are that shrew'd and knauish spirit<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Cal'd Robin Good-fellow.

Are you not hee,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
That frights the maidens of the Villagree,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
Skim milke, and sometimes labour in the querne,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
And bootlesse make the breathlesse huswife cherne,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
And sometime make the drinke to beare no barme,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Misleade night-wanderers, laughing at their harme,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
Those that Hobgoblin call you, and sweet Pucke,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
You do their worke, and they shall haue good lucke.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
Are not you he?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>
Rob.

Thou speak'st aright;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
I am that merrie wanderer of the night:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/>

I iest to Oberon, and make him smile,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_14"/>
When I a fat and bean-fed horse beguile,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_15"/>
Neighing in likenesse of a silly foale,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_16"/>
And sometime lurke I in a Gossips bole,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_17"/>
In very likenesse of a roasted crab:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_18"/>

And when she drinkes, against her lips I bob,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_19"/>
And on her withered dewlop poure the Ale.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_20"/>

The wisest Aunt telling the saddest tale,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_21"/>
Sometime for three-foot stoole, mistaketh me,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_22"/>
Then slip I from her bum, downe topples she,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_23"/>
And tailour cries, and fals into a coffe.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_24"/>

And then the whole quire hold their hips, and loffe,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_25"/>
And waxen in their mirth, and neeze, and sweare,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_26"/>
A merrier houre was neuer wasted there.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_27"/>
But roome Fairy, heere comes Oberon<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_28"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Fair.
And heere my Mistris:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Would that he were gone.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>

Enter the King of Fairies at one doore with his traine, and the<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
Queene at<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
another with hers.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/> </g>
Ill met by Moone-light.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Proud Tytania<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/> </g>
What, iealous Oberon?
Fairy skip hence.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
I haue forsworne his bed and companie<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/> </g>
Tarrie rash Wanton; am not I thy Lord?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Qu.

Then I must be thy Lady: but I know<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
When thou wast stolne away from Fairy Land,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
And in the shape of Corin, sate all day,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
Playing on pipes of Corne, and versing loue<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
To amorous Phillida.

Why art thou heere<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
Come from the farthest steepe of India?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>

But that forsooth the bouncing Amazon<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
Your buskin'd Mistresse, and your Warrior loue,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
To Theseus must be Wedded; and you come,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
To giue their bed ioy and prosperitie<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/> </g>
How canst thou thus for shame Tytania.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Glance at my credite, with Hippolita?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Knowing I know thy loue to Theseus?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>

Didst thou not leade him through the glimmering night<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
From Peregenia, whom he rauished?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>

And make him with faire Eagles breake his faith<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
With Ariadne, and Antiopa?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Que.

These are the forgeries of iealousie,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
And neuer since the middle Summers spring<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
Met we on hil, in dale, forrest, or mead,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
By paued fountaine, or by rushie brooke,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>
Or in the beached margent of the sea,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
To dance our ringlets to the whistling Winde,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/>
But with thy braules thou hast disturb'd our sport.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_14"/>

Therefore the Windes, piping to vs in vaine,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_15"/>
As in reuenge, haue suck'd vp from the sea<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_16"/>
Contagious fogges:

Which falling in the Land,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_17"/>
Hath euerie petty Riuer made so proud,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_18"/>
That they haue ouer-borne their Continents.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_19"/>

The Oxe hath therefore stretch'd his yoake in vaine,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_20"/>
The Ploughman lost his sweat, and the greene Corne<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_21"/>
Hath rotted, ere his youth attain'd a beard:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_22"/>

The fold stands empty in the drowned field,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_23"/>
And Crowes are fatted with the murrion flocke,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_24"/>
The nine mens Morris is fild vp with mud,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_25"/>
And the queint Mazes in the wanton greene,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_26"/>
For lacke of tread are vndistinguishable.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_27"/>

The humane mortals want their winter heere,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_28"/>
No night is now with hymne or caroll blest;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_29"/>
Therefore the Moone (the gouernesse of floods)<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_30"/>
Pale in her anger, washes all the aire;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_31"/>
That Rheumaticke diseases doe abound.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_32"/>

And through this distemperature, we see<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_33"/>
The seasons alter; hoared headed Frosts<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_34"/>
Fall in the fresh lap of the crimson Rose,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_35"/>
And on old Hyems chinne and Icie crowne,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_36"/>
An odorous Chaplet of sweet Sommer buds<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_37"/>
Is as in mockry set.

The Spring, the Sommer,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_38"/>
The childing Autumne, angry Winter change<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_39"/>
Their wonted Liueries, and the mazed world,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_40"/>
By their increase, now knowes not which is which;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_41"/>
And this same progeny of euills,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_42"/>
Comes from our debate, from our dissention,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_43"/>
We are their parents and originall<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_44"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Ober.

Do you amend it then, it lies in you,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Why should Titania crosse her Oberon?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>

I do but beg a little changeling boy,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
To be my Henchman<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/> </g>

Set your heart at rest,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
The Fairy land buyes not the childe of me,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
His mother was a Votresse of my Order,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
And in the spiced Indian aire, by night<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
Full often hath she gossipt by my side,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
And sat with me on Neptunes yellow sands,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
Marking th' embarked traders on the flood,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
When we haue laught to see the sailes conceiue,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
And grow big bellied with the wanton winde:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>

Which she with pretty and with swimming gate,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
Following (her wombe then rich with my yong squire)<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>
Would imitate, and saile vpon the Land,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
To fetch me trifles, and returne againe,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/>
As from a voyage, rich with merchandize.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_14"/>

But she being mortall, of that boy did die,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_15"/>
And for her sake I doe reare vp her boy,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_16"/>
And for her sake I will not part with him<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_17"/> </g>
How long within this wood intend you stay?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Qu.
Perchance till after Theseus wedding day.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>

If you will patiently dance in our Round,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
And see our Moone-light reuels, goe with vs;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
If not, shun me and I will spare your haunts<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/> </g>
Giue me that boy, and I will goe with thee</g>
Not for thy Fairy Kingdome.
Fairies away:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
We shall chide downe right, if I longer stay.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/> </g>
<g id="_0">Exeunt</g>
<g id="_0">Scanner's Notes:</g>

Wel, go thy way: thou shalt not from this groue,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Till I torment thee for this iniury.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>

My gentle Pucke come hither; thou remembrest<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
Since once I sat vpon a promontory,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
And heard a Meare-maide on a Dolphins backe,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
Vttering such dulcet and harmonious breath,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
That the rude sea grew ciuill at her song,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
And certaine starres shot madly from their Spheares,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
To heare the Sea-maids musicke<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Puc.
I remember</g>

That very time I say (but thou couldst not)<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Flying betweene the cold Moone and the earth,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Cupid all arm'd; a certaine aime he tooke<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
At a faire Vestall, throned by the West,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
And loos'd his loue-shaft smartly from his bow,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
As it should pierce a hundred thousand hearts,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
But I might see young Cupids fiery shaft<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Quencht in the chaste beames of the watry Moone;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
And the imperiall Votresse passed on,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
In maiden meditation, fancy free.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
Yet markt I where the bolt of Cupid fell.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>

It fell vpon a little westerne flower;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
Before, milke-white: now purple with loues wound,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/>
And maidens call it, Loue in idlenesse.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_14"/>

Fetch me that flower; the hearb I shew'd thee once,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_15"/>
The iuyce of it, on sleeping eye-lids laid,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_16"/>
Will make or man or woman madly dote<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_17"/>
Vpon the next liue creature that it sees.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_18"/>

Fetch me this hearbe, and be thou heere againe,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_19"/>
Ere the Leuiathan can swim a league<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_20"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Pucke.
Ile put a girdle about the earth, in forty minutes</g>
<g id="_0"> Ober.

Hauing once this iuyce,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Ile watch Titania, when she is asleepe,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
And drop the liquor of it in her eyes:<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>

The next thing when she waking lookes vpon,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
(Be it on Lyon, Beare, or Wolfe, or Bull,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
On medling Monkey, or on busie Ape)<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
Shee shall pursue it, with the soule of loue.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>

And ere I take this charme off from her sight,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>
(As I can take it with another hearbe)<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_9"/>
Ile make her render vp her Page to me.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_10"/>
But who comes heere?

I am inuisible,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_11"/>
And I will ouer-heare their conference.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_12"/>
Enter Demetrius, Helena following him.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_13"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Deme.

I loue thee not, therefore pursue me not,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
Where is Lysander, and faire Hermia?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
The one Ile stay, the other stayeth me.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>

Thou toldst me they were stolne into this wood;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
And heere am I, and wood within this wood,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
Because I cannot meet my Hermia.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>
Hence, get thee gone, and follow me no more<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Hel.

You draw me, you hard-hearted Adamant,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>
But yet you draw not Iron, for my heart<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Is true as steele.

Leaue you your power to draw,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
And I shall haue no power to follow you<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/> </g>
<g id="_0"> Deme.
Do I entice you? do I speake you faire?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_1"/>

Or rather doe I not in plainest truth,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_2"/>
Tell you I doe not, nor I cannot loue you?<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_3"/>
Hel.

And euen for that doe I loue thee the more;<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_4"/>
I am your spaniell, and Demetrius,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_5"/>
The more you beat me, I will fawne on you.<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_6"/>

Vse me but as your spaniell; spurne me, strike me,<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_7"/>
Neglect me, lose me; onely giue me leaue<x ctype="x-html-br" equiv-text="" id="_8"/>

<g id="_0">You will find a lot of these kinds of "errors" in this text, as I have mentioned in other times and places, many "scholars" have an extreme attachment to these errors, and many have accorded them a very high place in the "canon" of Shakespeare.
My father read an assortment of these made available to him by Cambridge University in England for several months in a glass room constructed for the purpose.

To the best of my knowledge he read ALL those available . . .in great detail. . .and determined from the various changes, that Shakespeare most likely did not write in nearly as many of a variety of errors we credit him for, even though he was in/famous for signing his name with several different spellings.</g>
